name: transparent overlay autotile for the edges of a cracked concrete slab pavement on dirt: only the broken edge is drawn — rounded dirt bites eaten into the concrete from the open sides, a dark 1px broken lip under south breaks, lit broken rims, and loose concrete chunks lying on the dirt; the slab field underneath shows through so its seams and cracks run right up to the break
label: wasteland_ruins/slab-break

surfaces.part: concrete slab fragments seen from above, flat floor decal on dirt

answer.evidence: The candidate is a flat overlay tile: dirt background with grey concrete slab patches seen straight from above. The patches have thin dark 1px lips on their south and west edges, but these are outlines rather than vertical faces, so there is no front face of 3+ rows. The silhouette is full-width (256) on every row, so there is no standing volume. This matches the flat kind (a plate or decal seen from above), and a flat decal is correctly a top-down slab with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has no flat fills: near-flat coverage is 0%, and the dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so the broken lips read as a dark brown-grey of the material rather than a black sticker line. It is also well built structurally, with rounded bites, lit rims, a dark south lip, chunks lying on the dirt and seams running up to the break. The shading is shallow, though. The concrete ramp has about 4 steps (light rim, mid grey with dither speckle, dark seam or lip), against about 6-7 on the paving reference. The dirt reads as about 3 tones of dark dots on a brown base. The whole sheet uses only 12 distinct colours, and a tile shows 5 visible tones against 7 for the paving reference. That is above the grass reference (3) but below the paving reference, which is the closer match for concrete. Chunks and slab faces rely on a light noise dither instead of stones or plates shaded one by one, with no per-chunk highlight steps. Since it is a little thinner than the paving reference and the rule is to fail when in doubt, it fails.

surfaces.part: concrete slab fragments and dirt-bite edges (flat overlay seen from above)

answer.evidence: This is a flat ground-decal autotile sheet, 256 px wide and 192 rows tall, with silhouette width 256 on every row. It shows dirt with irregular concrete patches seen straight down. The only vertical-looking marks are 1px dark broken lips under south breaks, which are outlines and not a front face of 3 or more rows. The column scan shows repeating 64-row tile cycles of dirt and concrete bands with no eave, no ellipse and no front face. This fits a flat overlay of the requested kind and reads as a top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has no flat fills: dirt and concrete both carry dither speckle, and near-flat coverage is 0%. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the lips and outlines lean brown or blue-grey. That fits the dark-material-tone outline. The weakness is ramp depth. The whole sheet uses only 12 colours and 5 visible tones per tile, against 7 on the paving reference. The concrete pieces read as about 4 steps (light rim, mid, speckle, dark lip). The paving reference has about 6 plus per-stone highlights. The dirt is a noisy 3-4 tone brown, and the concrete chunks are mostly uniform mid-grey dither without per-chunk shading. They look thinner and more like cut-out stickers than the Beodeul paving. The piece is clean and has no flat fills, but it is slightly below the reference, so it fails.

surfaces.part: concrete slab patches with broken dirt-bite edges, seams and cracks
loose concrete chunks and dark 1px broken lips on the dirt

answer.evidence: The tile is a full 256x192 ground overlay seen straight from above. The concrete patches are flat plates with seams, cracks and ragged dirt-bite edges. The only dark lines are 1px broken lips, such as the dark rows at the south breaks, and these are outlines rather than a vertical face. No front face of 3 or more rows is drawn, and there are no eave, ellipse or roof surfaces. This is a flat decal, so the whole thing is a top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate uses only 12 distinct colours in total. The concrete ramp has about 4 steps (light grey, mid grey, darker grey, dark lip), against roughly 6-7 in the paving reference. The dirt has about 3-4 browns in blotchy clumps. Measured tones per tile are 5, above the grass (3) but below the paving (7). Near-flat coverage is 0%, and the dark edge pixels are tinted rather than neutral (0% neutral), so the lip reads as a dark material tone and not a black sticker line. The concrete is speckled and has seam lines. The chunks and bites are fairly small, simple blobs with little per-chunk highlight and shadow variation, and the lit rims are thin. Overall it is cleanly made but shallower than the Beodeul paving in ramp depth and texture, and with no clear case for a pass I fail it.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete slab fragments and dirt-bite edges lying flat on dirt, seen from above

answer.evidence: The tile is a flat overlay of concrete slab patches and chunks on a dirt background, viewed straight down. The thin dark 1px lips under south breaks are outline-like edge details, not a vertical front face of 3 or more rows. The object has no standing volume, so the kind (flat) matches and it reads as a flat top-down plate with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 5 visible tones per tile, against 7 for the paving reference and 3 for grass. Near-flat coverage is 0% and the dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so the outline is not a sticker line. However, the whole piece uses only 12 distinct colours. The concrete ramp is shallow, about 4 steps (light, mid, speckle, dark lip/crack) against roughly 6 in the paving reference. The rims and chunks read mostly as a single grey with light speckle, with little per-chunk highlight and shadow shaping. The dirt is a repetitive blob pattern in about 3-4 browns, closer to the grass reference's tone count but without its tuft variety. Overall it is competent and not flat, but thinner in shading depth than the Beodeul paving standard, and with that doubt it fails.
